headline: Dōryō is borrowed from Middle Chinese 同僚 (MC duwng lew).
Sasayaku is ささ (sasa, an onomatopoeia) plus the verb-forming suffix やく (-yaku).
Juwaki is 受話 (juwa, “listening on a telephone”) plus 器 (-ki, “device”).
Michijun is 道 (michi, “way”) plus 順 (jun, “order”).
Noru, “to appear in print”, is cognate with 乗る (noru).
Hokori, “pride”, is the continuative stem of 誇る (hokoru, “to be proud of”).
Kasanaru is from Old Japanese; compare 嵩む (kasamu, “to increase”).
Shimatta is the perfective of しまう (shimau, “to finish”): literally “finished”.
Kumu, “to serve sake”, is likely the same word as 汲む (kumu, “to pour”).
Hikkakaru is a sound shift from ひきかかる (hikikakaru).
Dan, “step”, is from Middle Chinese 段.
Kōsa is Middle Chinese 交叉, with 差 a daiyōji replacing 叉.
Kaikan is from Chinese 會館 (huìguǎn), analyzable as 会 (kai, “meeting; gathering”) plus 館 (kan, “public building”).
Neru is from Old Japanese 寝 (nu).
Zen, “good”, is from Middle Chinese 善.
Oshimai is 御 (o-, beautifying prefix) plus しまい (shimai, “ending, finishing”).
Mukau is a shift from 向き合う (mukiau).
Kantai, the “frigid zone”, is 寒 (“cold”) plus 帯 (“belt”).
Oikosu is 追う (ou, “to chase”) plus 越す (kosu, “to go past”).
Aratamete is the -te form of the verb 改める (aratameru).
Nashi is the classical terminal form of the modern adjective 無い (nai).
Kappu is English cup, a doublet via Late Latin cuppa of コップ (koppu).
Osoroshii is an adjectivization of the verb 恐る (osoru, “to fear”).
Masatsu is a Middle Chinese compound, 摩擦 (MC ma tshat).
Bushu, “radical”, is from Middle Chinese 部首, first mentioned in Chinese in the Shūowén Jiězì of roughly 100 CE.
Arai is cognate with 粗い (arai).
Fukuramu, “to swell”, is 膨 (fukura, “a bulge, a swelling”) plus -mu, first cited to the mid-800s.
Massaki is 真っ (ma'-, “truly”) plus 先 (saki, “first”).
Ji, “character”, is from Middle Chinese 字.
Sakeru is from 避く (saku), cognate with 裂ける (sakeru).
Kō, “this way”, shifted from 斯く (kaku): kaku, kau, kɔː, then kō.
